name: LM2775DSGR
title: LM2775 regulated switched-capacitor 5 V boost converter, 200 mA, 2 MHz, WSON-8
summary: A charge-pump doubler with built-in regulation that makes a fixed 5 V rail from a 2.7 V to 5.5 V input using one flying capacitor plus input and output capacitors, no inductor. It delivers 200 mA from 3.1 V to 5.5 V and 125 mA at 2.7 V, switching at 2 MHz. A PFM pin selects pulse-frequency operation for low quiescent current at light load, and an OUTDIS pin chooses whether the output is actively discharged or left high-impedance in shutdown. Input current limit, thermal shutdown and undervoltage lockout are built in; named uses are USB OTG, HDMI power and portable equipment.
key_figures: 5 V fixed (4.8 V min, 5.2 V max at IOUT = 180 mA)
200 mA for VIN 3.1 V to 5.5 V; 125 mA at VIN = 2.7 V
75 µA typ with PFM = '1'; 5 mA typ with PFM = '0'

notes: An automotive Q100 version, LM2775-Q1, exists under its own part number.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit
circuits.description: The minimum LM2775 circuit: a 2.7 V to 5.5 V source feeds VIN with a 2.2 µF capacitor to ground, a 1 µF flying capacitor sits between C1+ and C1-, and a 2.2 µF capacitor holds up the 5 V output, good for up to 200 mA. EN, PFM and OUTDIS are brought out as control inputs.

circuits.title: Typical LM2775 configuration
circuits.description: A battery-powered 5 V, 200 mA supply for a downstream system. PFM and OUTDIS are tied to the battery rail along with VIN, so PFM operation is allowed at light load and the output is discharged whenever the part is off. A controller drives EN to turn the rail on and off. Input and output capacitors are 10 µF and the flying capacitor 1 µF.

circuits.title: USB OTG configuration
circuits.description: The LM2775 supplies VBUS for a dual-role USB port in host mode. VIN and PFM run from the system battery rail and OUTDIS is grounded, so when the application processor pulls EN low the output goes high-impedance and another source may drive VBUS. The 5 V output feeds both the USB OTG transceiver and the VBUS pin of the connector; the transceiver carries ID, D+ and D- to the connector and talks to the processor.

equations.note: At 2 MHz with 1 µF the 1/(FSW × C1) term is about 0.5 Ω, so the switch term dominates.

equations.name: Efficiency, ideal
equations.expr: IIN = G × IOUT; E = (VOUT × IOUT) / (VIN × IIN) = VOUT / (G × VIN)
equations.note: Quiescent current and other losses are left out. Efficiency is highest as G × VIN nears VOUT.

equations.name: Efficiency with quiescent current
equations.expr: E = POUT / PIN = (VOUT × IOUT) / (VIN × (2 × IOUT + IQ))

equations.name: Power dissipation
equations.expr: PD = PIN - POUT = [VIN × (2 × IOUT + IQ)] - [VOUT × IOUT]
equations.note: Reaches 1.35 W at VIN = 5.5 V and IOUT = 200 mA.

equations.note: Takes the output capacitor as carrying the whole load for half a switching period.

equations.name: Output ripple, with non-overlap and ESR
equations.note: The output capacitor carries the load for about 60 % of a switching period once the non-overlap time between phases is counted.

operation.text: The LM2775 combines a switched-capacitor doubler with linear regulation. An internal two-phase clock with non-overlapping phases runs four switches. During φ1 C1 sits between VIN and ground and charges up to VIN; during φ2 it is stacked on top of VIN and switched onto the output, raising the output and feeding the load. Regulation comes from controlling the current in the two switches on the VIN side, one used in each phase.
Because the current through the VIN-side switches is controlled before the voltage is doubled, the input current carries very little ripple, and little noise is put back onto the supply line.

Excess input current or a short from the output to ground is limited; with the output shorted directly to ground the input current is held at 600 mA typical. Dissipation is high in this state and thermal cycling is to be expected.

With PFM high, the pump switches only when VOUT has fallen to about 5.05 V, which keeps quiescent current low at light load. Pulse rate has no lower bound and falls under 1 kHz unloaded; it rises as the load grows. With PFM low the part switches at a constant 2 MHz, giving lower output ripple and a predictable frequency, at the cost of a higher quiescent current at light load.

When EN goes low after running, OUTDIS sets what the output does. With OUTDIS low the output is left high-impedance and stays up, so the LM2775 can share a rail that another source also drives, as on a USB OTG bus; it then draws about 1.6 µA typical from that rail. With OUTDIS high the part pulls the output down until it reaches ground, drawing roughly 450 µA from the output.

The part shuts down when the junction reaches 150 °C typical and restarts once it has cooled to 130 °C typical. Self-heating from high input voltage and output current is the usual trigger, and the result is thermal cycling, seen as a pulsing output. Lowering the input voltage, output current or ambient temperature, or improving heat removal through the board, stops it. The WSON package soldered to a board laid out for heat spreading supports high dissipation.
A comparator on VIN puts the part into shutdown when the input drops to 2.4 V and lets it run again once the input climbs above 2.6 V.

The part is in shutdown when VIN is removed or falls toward ground, or when EN is driven low with VIN in its normal range. Supply current in shutdown is typically under 1 µA. Depending on OUTDIS the output is pulled low (OUTDIS = '1') or held near its last value with low leakage (OUTDIS = '0').
With VIN in range and EN high the part regulates, either in PFM bursts (PFM = '1') or by constant switching (PFM = '0').

Full 200 mA output is available for VIN from 3.1 V to 5.5 V. The part can be modelled as a linear pre-regulator, then an ideal doubler, then an output resistance ROUT of 3.5 Ω typical, roughly double the on-resistance of its four switches. While in regulation the pre-regulator raises its output V' as load increases so that VOUT holds at 5 V ± 4 %. Once V' has risen all the way to VIN, further load pulls VOUT down in proportion to ROUT, as in an unregulated doubler. Power dissipation and thermal effects deserve care in high-current use, especially at high input voltage.

Raising the flying capacitance above 1 µF gains little output current, since the switch resistance dominates ROUT. It may be reduced below 1 µF to save size or cost, provided ROUT does not rise enough to cause unwanted droop. With ceramic capacitors ESR is negligible, typically far under 100 mΩ. Too small a flying capacitor can leave the part unable to regulate at high load; too large a one can overpower the input and output capacitors and raise ripple at both. 1 µF low-ESR ceramic is the recommended value for high-current use. C1 must never be a polarised type (tantalum, aluminium electrolytic), since it can see reverse bias in operation.

Three external capacitors are required, and surface-mount multilayer ceramics are recommended for their small size, low cost and very low ESR (15 mΩ or less typical). Tantalum, OS-CON and aluminium electrolytic parts are generally not recommended because of their higher ESR. X7R and X5R dielectrics are preferred: tolerance as tight as ±10 %, and ±15 % over -55 °C to 125 °C (X7R) or -55 °C to 85 °C (X5R). Y5V and Z5U are generally not recommended: their tolerance spans 80 % to 20 % and they drift +22 %/-82 % (Y5V, -30 °C to 85 °C) or +22 %/-56 % (Z5U, 10 °C to 85 °C), so a 1 µF part may fall to 0.1 µF and miss the minimum capacitance the LM2775 needs. Ceramic capacitance also falls with DC bias, which raises ripple; running well below the rated voltage reduces this. Evaluation with the production capacitors early in design is strongly recommended. The output capacitor should be rated 10 V or more; the others at or above the highest input voltage.

Output ripple is set mainly by COUT and scales inversely with it; VIN, load and C1 also have an effect. During the charge phase the load runs from COUT alone. A 10 µF, 10 V low-ESR ceramic is recommended for high-current use. Changing COUT may call for changing the flying and input capacitors too. With a small output capacitor and PFM enabled, ripple can become large around the switch-over between PFM and constant switching; 2 µF of effective capacitance is recommended to stop this toggling. A 10 µF, 10 V 0402 capacitor typically has only about 2 µF left at 5 V bias. A high-ESR output capacitor such as tantalum raises ripple; a low-ESR ceramic in parallel brings the net ESR down.

CIN supplies the charge drawn by the flying capacitor at the start of each charge phase, keeps VIN from dipping then, and filters noise away from the internal analog circuits that run from VIN. Input ripple scales inversely with CIN and depends to a lesser degree on VIN, load current and C1. A 10 µF low-ESR ceramic is recommended for high-current use; changing it may call for changing the flying and output capacitors as well.

For this use OUTDIS is tied to ground and only EN is driven. In host mode EN is high and the LM2775 supplies the 5 V bus; in device mode EN is low, the output is high-impedance, and an outside supply may drive the bus without back-driving the part. The 250 mA typical output current limit sits within USB OTG and HDMI needs.

The input supply must lie between 2.7 V and 5.5 V, be well regulated and be able to deliver the input current needed. If it is far from the LM2775, bulk capacitance may be needed alongside the ceramic bypass capacitors.

Put all capacitors as near the LM2775 as possible, ideally on the board side the part is on. Join them to the part with short, wide traces to keep resistance and inductance low. Give the GND pin a low-resistance path to ground, best done with wide traces or several vias into a ground plane. The thermal pad and GND pin both connect to the ground plane; the input and output capacitors sit by the GND, VIN and VOUT pins on one side and the flying capacitor across C1- and C1+ on the other.

The exposed thermal pad is soldered to the board for both heat removal and mechanical strength. Vias in the pad are optional; where used they sit at the positions of the land pattern and are filled, plugged or tented if under paste.
